topic: Feeds & lists: pagination, prefetching & list performance

questions.question: A social feed gets new posts at the top every few seconds. Why does it usually page with a cursor (e.g. `after=<lastPostId>`) instead of `?offset=40&limit=20`?
options: Cursors let the client jump straight to any page number, which offsets cannot do without loading earlier pages
Cursor paging returns smaller payloads because the server leaves out fields that are already on the device
Offset responses cannot be cached by OkHttp or URLSession, while cursor-based responses can be cached normally
New posts shift every offset, so offset paging returns duplicates or skips items; a cursor anchors to the last item seen
questions.explanation: With offsets, inserting 5 posts at the top means 'offset 40' now starts 5 items earlier, so the user sees repeats (or misses items on deletes). A cursor says 'items after this one', which stays correct while the list changes. Cursors are actually worse at random page jumps, and caching or payload size have nothing to do with the choice.

questions.question: In Paging 3, combining a Room-backed PagingSource with a RemoteMediator makes the database the single source of truth: the network only writes pages into Room, and the UI pages from Room.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: RemoteMediator loads from the network when Paging reaches the end of the local data and inserts the results into Room; the Room PagingSource invalidates and the UI re-pages from the DB. That gives offline support and consistent data. On iOS there is no built-in equivalent, so teams usually page manually with a cursor and observe Core Data / SwiftData or GRDB results.

questions.question: Why do lists use diffing with stable IDs (ListAdapter/DiffUtil, LazyColumn `key`, or UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource) instead of reloading the whole list when data changes?
options: Diffing makes the network layer request only rows that changed, which cuts the size of each page response
Diffing lets the list skip measuring rows that are offscreen, which a plain reload would always measure again
The framework can update only changed rows, animate moves and inserts, and keep per-row state such as scroll or focus
Pagination cannot work without diffing, because the next page has to be merged into the list on the server
questions.explanation: A full reload rebinds every visible row, drops animations and can reset state; diffing by ID finds the minimal set of inserts, removes, moves and changes. It is purely a UI concern and has nothing to do with what the network fetches. Skipping offscreen rows comes from virtualization (recycling / lazy layout), not from diffing.

questions.question: Users who fling quickly through a feed keep hitting a loading spinner at the bottom, even though each page loads in about 400 ms. What is the best first fix?
options: Start loading the next page earlier, i.e. raise the prefetch distance so the request fires a few screens before the end
Replace the spinner with a shimmer placeholder so the wait feels shorter while keeping the paging logic as is
Load every page in the background on app start so all of the feed is already cached before the user scrolls
Raise the page size to 500 items so a single request covers almost every scrolling session without paging
questions.explanation: If a 400 ms load is visible, the trigger is simply too late for the scroll speed; Paging 3's `prefetchDistance` (or `UICollectionViewDataSourcePrefetching` / a 'near end' check on iOS) moves it earlier. Huge pages slow the first load and waste data, and preloading everything wastes battery and bandwidth. A shimmer is cosmetic and does not remove the wait.

questions.question: A product list drops frames while scrolling. Which are likely causes worth checking first? Select all that apply.
options: Using cursor-based pagination, because comparing cursors on each scroll event costs more than an offset check
Items without stable keys, so every data update rebinds or recomposes all visible rows
RecyclerView recycling its views, since re-attaching a recycled view is slower than inflating a fresh one
Per-row work during bind or composition, such as date formatting, regex parsing or building spans, done every frame
Decoding images at full resolution instead of downsampling to the cell size, or doing it on the main thread
questions.explanation: Oversized image decodes, unstable keys and heavy work in bind/compose are the classic sources of scroll jank on both platforms (the same applies to `cellForItemAt` on iOS). The paging scheme runs once per page, not per frame. Recycling exists precisely because reusing a view is far cheaper than inflating a new one.

questions.question: A LazyColumn uses `items(list)` with no `key`. Each row has `var expanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }`. The user expands row 3, then a new item is inserted at the top. What happens?
options: The expanded state stays with position 3, so a different item now appears expanded; adding `key = { it.id }` fixes it
The app throws an IllegalStateException because the list changed size while rows held remembered state
All remembered row states are discarded on any data change, so every row collapses back to its default state
Compose notices the inserted item by comparing elements with equals() and moves the expanded state to the right row
questions.explanation: Without keys, lazy items are identified by index, so `remember` state belongs to slot 3 rather than to the item that was there. A stable key ties state (and scroll anchoring) to the item's identity. Compose does not diff your items by equality on its own; the key is how you tell it identity.

questions.question: Cursor-based pagination on its own makes it cheap for the client to show 'page 37 of 120' and jump straight to page 37.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A cursor only tells you where to continue from, so reaching page 37 means walking the pages before it, and a total count needs a separate (often expensive) query. That is why cursors suit infinite feeds while offset or keyed page numbers suit admin-style tables with page jumps. Pick based on the UX, not by habit.

questions.question: A user is 60 posts deep in a feed when 8 new posts arrive over the socket. What is the best behaviour?
options: Store them locally but show a 'New posts' pill, keep the scroll anchored, and insert them when the user taps or returns to top
Throw away the current pages and reload the feed from the newest post so ordering is guaranteed to be correct
Insert them at the top immediately so the feed is always fresh, and let the list scroll as the content above it grows
Ignore them until the next cold start, because live inserts into a paged list always break the paging keys
questions.explanation: Inserting above the viewport shifts what the user is reading, which feels like a bug; the pill pattern (used by most social apps) gives freshness without losing place. Reloading drops the user's position and wastes data. With a DB-backed list and stable keys, inserts are perfectly safe; it is a UX choice when to reveal them.

questions.question: On pull-to-refresh your RemoteMediator deletes the items table, commits, then inserts page 1 and its remote keys in a second transaction. Users see the list flash empty and sometimes paging stops. What is the fix?
options: Call `adapter.refresh()` twice in a row so the second refresh fills the list before the empty frame is drawn
Switch the remote API to offset paging so remote keys are no longer needed and the second write disappears
Do the delete, the new items and the remote keys in one database transaction so observers never see a half-updated state
Turn off placeholders in PagingConfig so the empty table is not rendered while the second transaction runs
questions.explanation: Room invalidates the PagingSource on each committed transaction, so the UI briefly pages an empty table, and if the process dies between the two writes the remote keys no longer match the items. Wrapping everything in `withTransaction` makes the swap atomic. The other options change symptoms or the API but leave the non-atomic write in place.

questions.question: A feed has mixed-height cards with large images. Which measures reduce layout shift and jank? Select all that apply.
options: Let image views wrap their content and grow when the bitmap arrives, so each card always matches its image
Fetch every image at its original resolution so a single cached copy can serve every screen density
Prefetch images for the next few items (Coil/Glide preload, Kingfisher/SDWebImage prefetcher) into the caches
Cancel image requests for cards that scroll off screen so they do not compete with the visible ones
Return image dimensions or aspect ratio in the API so each card reserves its final size before the image loads
questions.explanation: Reserving space from known dimensions prevents content jumping, prefetching hides network latency, and cancelling offscreen work keeps bandwidth and decode time for what is visible. Wrap-content images are exactly what causes cards to resize mid-scroll. Original-resolution images waste data and memory; request a size close to the display size, e.g. via a CDN resize parameter.
